metadata.note: The Bath and Hammondsport Railroad, Steuben County, New York: a 9-mile steam short line from Bath, on the Erie and the DL&W, to Hammondsport at the head of Keuka Lake, built to carry passengers to the Keuka Lake steamers and grapes and wine out. Chartered Jan 17 1872, opened June 30 1875 as a 3 ft narrow gauge, standard-gauged Aug 1889, Erie-controlled from 1903/1908 to 1935-36. Regular passenger service drawn 1875-1917 [OPEN]. Nicknamed 'The Champagne Route' (a slogan, not a train name). Research report: research/branches/bath_and_hammondsport_railroad.txt.

metadata.operator_split: None drawn. Lessees Allen Wood (1874/75-1886) and Henry Stebbins (1886-?) worked the line as the B&H. Erie control (1903 per Palmer/Wikipedia, by 1908 per Jackson/American-Rails) appears to have been stock control - the B&H stayed a separate company (sold as the B&H in 1936; own entry in the 1951 Official Guide). If a source shows the Erie operated the passenger trains, split at 1903 into an Erie feature, Erie colour pulled programmatically.
omitted: Report block [2] (drawable: NONE): the July 25 1936 'Wine Special', undated 1940s NRHS excursions, and the 1993-1994 Champagne Railroad excursions (which ran on the county-owned ex-DL&W Bath - Wayland line, not established as reaching Hammondsport).

All freight-only years: Bath - Hammondsport after regular passenger service ended (freight and express only by Aug 1951; freight under the B&H and B&H Rail Corp thereafter), and B&H Rail Corp's freight operation of the ex-DL&W Bath - Wayland and NS Painted Post - Bath lines (Rule 1).
The run of a few tenths of a mile over the shared Erie/DL&W corridor to the Bath depots (depot sites not located; see geometry_quality).

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced throughout from OpenStreetMap (Overpass, maps.mail.ru mirror, 2026-10-17) with opstrace.py; no approximated (straight-line) legs. 8.2 mi traced against 9 mi documented (Official Guide Feb 1952 company entry) and 9.2 mi Bath (DL&W depot) - Hammondsport / 9.0 mi from the Bath Erie depot (Fowler) - about 9% short. The shortfall is at the Bath end: the line is drawn from where the B&H's own track leaves the shared Erie/DL&W corridor in south-east Bath (42.3270, -77.3110); the B&H's run of a few tenths of a mile over that corridor to the Bath depots is NOT drawn, because neither depot's site was located (Fowler's Lackawanna Street 1.0 / Washington Street 1.3 mileposts could not be reconciled with the modern street crossings). Every traced mile is on ways tagged old_railway_operator=Erie and tiger:name_base 'Bath and Hammondsport Railroad' (name 'B&H Rail Corporation'): rail/spur from Bath to near the Fish Hatchery, railway=disused through Pleasant Valley to Rheims, and railway=abandoned (rails lifted 2008) Rheims - Hammondsport lake front. LATER ALIGNMENT: this is the surviving standard-gauge alignment. The line was built 3 ft gauge and re-laid to standard gauge in Aug 1889; whether the 1875-1889 narrow-gauge line followed exactly the same alignment (curves, Bath approach) is not established, so the 1875-1889 segment may be drawn on a slightly later alignment.

segments.note: Bath (connection with the Erie and the DL&W) up the Cohocton valley and Pleasant Valley to Hammondsport at the south end of Keuka Lake, where trains met the lake steamers. Built 3 ft gauge; completed and opened June 30 1875 (Jackson, RGVRRM; American-Rails) by lessee Allen Wood, who held a 99-year lease from Dec 15 1874; lease passed to Henry Stebbins Nov 15 1886 - individuals working the B&H under its own name, not a change of company. Steam from opening; no animal traction recorded. Rail City Museum's 'first train ... summer of 1874' conflicts with the June 1875 opening and is probably a construction train (rail was laid only after the Dec 1874 lease). Segment ends at the August 1889 regauging (Jackson: track re-laid Aug 17 1889; American-Rails: reopened Aug 1 1889 - dates conflict; a weeks-long closure, not a gap in drawn years). Headway is an ESTIMATE: the only frequency found, '10 trips a day' (Sherer), is an undated peak figure.
sources: Segment-level: opening June 30 1875 (Jackson, RGVRRM; American-Rails), corroborated by Fowler's 1875 Official Guide letter 'y' on Bath and Hammondsport; 3 ft gauge and Aug 1889 regauging (Jackson, American-Rails, Wikipedia, Fowler 'ex 3' 0" gauge'). Headway NOT sourced - estimate.

segments.note: Standard gauge from Aug 1889. Erie Railroad stock control from 1903 (Palmer; Wikipedia 'around 1903') or by 1908 (Jackson; American-Rails) - the B&H kept its own corporate identity, so this is not drawn as an Erie feature (see metadata.not_yet_sourced). At its height '10 trips a day to Hammondsport', up to 12 in grape season (Sherer, undated); headway_min is an ESTIMATE from that figure. Passenger business was killed by the automobile; Palmer (Crooked Lake Review, Nov 1994) dates its discontinuance to 1917, 'about the same time the Keuka Lake steamers ceased operation', with a few coaches kept for special events. END IS [OPEN]: 1917 is the earliest end any source asserts and the last year treated as CONFIRMED - it is not a known end. Jackson (RGVRRM) says passenger service 'continued into the mid-1920s'; neither source cites a timetable or a dated last train. Do not extend without evidence (an Official Guide of c.1920-1930 or a 'last passenger train' newspaper story). Context, not drawn: USRA control from Jan 1918; July 8 1935 flood washout near the Fish Hatchery and Erie abandonment approval Aug 23 1935; sold to Hammondsport businessmen and reopened July 4 1936 as a freight and express road (Official Guide Aug 1951: 'Freight and express service', Hammondsport daggered freight-only); a one-off 'Wine Special' July 25 1936 and undated 1940s NRHS excursions; freight continued under the B&H and its successors.
sources: Segment-level: start = Aug 1889 standard-gauge reopening (Jackson; American-Rails); end 1917 per Palmer, Crooked Lake Review Nov 1994 (and Wikipedia, which probably follows Palmer) - conflicts with Jackson (RGVRRM) 'mid-1920s'; [OPEN] end. Peak frequency from Sherer (undated). Headway is an estimate.
